passages.happening:
‘Then Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to take a census of Israel’ (verse 1). David tells Joab and the commanders to count the Israelites from Beersheba to Dan, ‘so that I may know their number’ (verse 2). Joab objects: “My lord the king, are they not all servants of my lord? Why does my lord want to do this? Why should he bring guilt on Israel?” (verse 3). ‘Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab’ (verse 4).

Joab reports 1,100,000 men who drew the sword in all Israel, 470,000 of them in Judah (verse 5), but he leaves out Levi and Benjamin, ‘because the king’s command was detestable to him’ (verse 6). ‘This command was also evil in the sight of God; so He struck Israel’ (verse 7). David says to God, “I have sinned greatly because I have done this thing. Now I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
After chapters of victory, this is the one sin of David that the Chronicler tells at length, and it matters because of where it leads. The story ends at a threshing floor where judgment stops and an altar is built, and the next verse says, ‘Here shall be the house of the LORD God’ (22:1). The temple's site is chosen not in a moment of triumph but in sin, repentance and mercy.

In the ancient Near East a census was usually taken for taxes or for conscription, and these are men who drew the sword. It asserted the king's control over the people's strength. The law required a ransom at a census so that no plague would come on the people, which suggests that counting Israel was understood as spiritually dangerous. Joab's question in verse 3, whether the people were not all the king's servants already, may hint that the census treated God's people as the king's own resource. The Bible does not say plainly why the census was sinful. Suggestions include pride and trust in military numbers rather than in God, a failure to pay the ransom the law required, and treating God's people as the king's possession. Joab's objection points toward the first and the last.

The numbers differ from 2 Samuel 24:9, which gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah; Chronicles adds that Levi and Benjamin were not counted. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel, Kings and Chronicles sets out the ways readers explain such differences, and these notes take no side beyond it.
passages.later: The law said, ‘each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted. Then no plague will come upon them when they are numbered’ (Exodus 30:12).
passages.hard:
Who incited David to take the census: God, as 2 Samuel 24:1 says, or Satan, as Chronicles says?

Second Samuel begins the same event, ‘Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them’ (2 Samuel 24:1). Chronicles says that Satan rose up and incited David. Readers account for the difference in more than one way, and each deserves to be heard in its own terms.

Many see both as true at different levels. God permitted or used the adversary's temptation to carry out a judgment already due, as in Job, where the accuser acts only with God's leave, while David freely chose his act and answered for it. On this reading the two books describe one event from two heights.

Others see a development in Israel's thought after the exile. The Chronicler, writing later, names a heavenly adversary behind the evil, so that God is not seen as its author. On this reading Samuel speaks in the older Hebrew way, in which everything that happens, even what God permits, can be called his doing.

Some take the Hebrew differently. The word satan means adversary or accuser, and it can name a human opponent, as it does elsewhere. Here it has no article, which many read as a personal name, Satan, while others translate it an adversary, perhaps a human enemy whose threat prompted David to count his troops.

All agree on one thing, and so does David: he was responsible. He says, “I have sinned greatly” (verse 8). The notes on 2 Samuel 24 take the same view, and neither book makes God the author of sin.
passages.asks: Joab saw the danger and said so, and David overruled him. Ask whose warning you have overruled because you wanted to know your own strength. And ask what you count, in money, numbers or followers, to feel secure.

passages.t: Three choices, a plague, and a king who pleads for his people
passages.happening:
Through the seer Gad, the LORD gives David three choices: three years of famine, three months of defeat by his enemies, or three days of plague (verses 9-12). David answers, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men” (verse 13). ‘So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell dead’ (verse 14).

God sends an angel against Jerusalem, ‘but as the angel was doing so, the LORD saw it and relented from the calamity’ (verse 15), and says to him, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” (verse 15). The angel stands by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. David sees him with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, and David and the elders, in sackcloth, fall facedown (verse 16). David prays, “I am the one who has sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? O LORD my God, please let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house, but do not let this plague remain upon Your people” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The story moves from sin to judgment, then to mercy and intercession. David chooses God's hand over human hands because of God's mercies, rachamim, a word related to the word for womb, with a sense of deep, almost bodily tenderness. He stakes everything on it.

The word for relented, nacham, used of God, describes a change in his declared action in response to repentance or prayer, not a change in his character. The LORD saw, and stopped the angel at the edge of Jerusalem. Sackcloth, a rough goat-hair cloth, was worn in mourning and repentance.

In 2 Samuel 24:13 the standard Hebrew text has seven years of famine; the Greek translation called the Septuagint has three, as Chronicles does, and the BSB follows it there. David is at his worst and at his best in the same chapter. He overrules good advice, then confesses fully, and when he sees the angel he offers himself and his own house in place of the people.
passages.later: Second Samuel tells the same prayer: ‘Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done?’ (2 Samuel 24:17).
passages.hard:
Why did seventy thousand people die for the king's sin?

This is the hardest part of the chapter, and the notes will not pretend otherwise. David himself raises the question in his prayer: these sheep, what have they done? The Bible lets his protest stand.

The text says more than one thing at once. In 2 Samuel the chapter begins with the LORD's anger against Israel, so the people are not presented simply as innocent bystanders, though their sin is never named. In both books the king's act is the trigger, and in the ancient world a king's act was the act of his people in a way that is hard for modern readers to feel. And in both books God cuts the plague short in mercy, before it reaches Jerusalem, while David is still pleading. None of these makes the deaths easy to read, and the chapter does not resolve every question. It holds God's rule, human responsibility and God's mercy together.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David prayed that the harm would fall on him and not on the people in his care. Ask who suffers when you do wrong, and whether you have asked for their sake. And ask what it means to trust God's mercy when you do not understand his judgment.

passages.happening:
The angel tells Gad to send David up to build an altar on Ornan's threshing floor (verse 18). Ornan, threshing wheat, sees the angel; his four sons hide (verse 20). When David arrives, Ornan bows and offers him everything: the oxen for burnt offerings, the threshing sledges for wood and the wheat for the grain offering (verse 23).

David answers, “I insist on paying the full price, for I will not take for the LORD what belongs to you, nor will I offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (verse 24). ‘So David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold for the site’ (verse 25). He builds an altar and calls on the LORD, ‘who answered him with fire from heaven on the altar of burnt offering’ (verse 26). The angel puts his sword back in its sheath (verse 27). David offers sacrifices there, because the tabernacle and its altar were at Gibeon, and ‘he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
A threshing floor was a flat, hard surface, often on high ground to catch the wind, where grain was beaten out and winnowed. Oxen pulled heavy sledges across the stalks. Ornan offered both for the sacrifice. Ornan, called Araunah in Samuel, was a Jebusite, one of the city's people from before David took it, still holding land there. The word goren, threshing floor, comes five times in the chapter, marking the place where judgment stops and worship begins.

Fire from heaven on an offering was a sign that God accepted it, as at the first sacrifice at the tabernacle and on Mount Carmel. The closing verses explain why this altar, not the tabernacle at Gibeon, became the place of Israel's worship.

The price differs from 2 Samuel 24:24, where David pays fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen. Some explain the smaller sum as the price of the floor and oxen and the larger as the price of the whole site around it. Others see the Chronicler stressing the worth of the temple's site. The threshing floor lay on the hill north of the old city of David, which 2 Chronicles 3:1 calls Mount Moriah, the name of the region where Abraham was sent to offer Isaac.
passages.later: Second Chronicles says that Solomon built the temple ‘on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David. This was the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite’ (2 Chronicles 3:1). Genesis names the region where Abraham was sent: ‘go to the land of Moriah’ (Genesis 22:2).
passages.asks: David would not offer to God what had cost him nothing. Ask what your worship costs you. And ask whether there is a place in your own life where judgment and mercy met, and what was built there.
